newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Bank of Canada in new era of independence.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bank of Canada in new era of independence.

text.p: Canada's flamboyant former Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau once said his country's relationship with the United States was like a mouse being in bed with an elephant.

Until this year that metaphor was an apt description of the Bank of Canada's relationship with the U.S. Federal Reserve. Canada's central bank has had little latitude in the past decade to uncouple its monetary policy from the Fed's even when the state of the economy warranted it.

But with the Fed's rate-setting Open Market Committee meeting tomorrow, and the scene set for a U.S. interest rate hike, many Canadians believe the traditional relationship between the two central banks is about to change.

"They (the Bank of Canada) clearly have enough flexibility and credibility that they can set their own course to a considerable extent, much more than in the past," said Jim Webber, director of fixed-income research for TD Securities Inc.
If the Fed raises U.S. short-term rates tomorrow, few market watchers expect the Bank of Canada to follow suit.
There is little fear that financial markets will punish the Canadian bank for standing pat in the face of a U.S. rate rise, as it did in late 1994.

The Bank of Canada's newfound independence from the Fed has been years in the making. The reasons for it include declining government deficits, the country's first current account surplus in 12 years and an inflation record that is the envy of the industrialized world.

"I think we've paid the price in terms of tough fiscal policy, tough trade policy and tough monetary policy so we can conduct our made in Canada monetary policy," said Michael Gregory, an economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers. "If it's justified by fundamentals, I think the markets will accept it,"

A drop in government borrowing is cited as the biggest reason for the increase in the Bank of Canada's independence from the Fed. Both federal and provincial governments have cut spending sharply over the past three years to control deficits that spiked sharply upward during the last recession.

Finance Minister Paul Martin confirmed last week that the budget deficit for 1995/96 would come in under C$30 billion -- well under his original C$32.7 billion target and down from a peak of C$42 billion in 1993/94.
Seven of Canada's 10 provinces are expected to balance their budgets this year.

Declining government borrowing helped contribute to Canada's first quarterly current account surplus in 12 years last month. The current account is a measure of a country's balance of payments with the rest of the world.
Analysts said Canada's 12-year record of current account deficits was largely the result of interest payments to foreign bondholders.

Bolstered by improved economic fundamentals, the Bank of Canada earlier this year began to move its monetary policy away from that of the Federal Reserve. The two countries' economies then seemed to be going in different directions.
The Fed put through its last rate cut on January 31, then held rates steady amid indications that the U.S. economy was running near full capacity.
In Canada, however, economic growth remained sluggish and economists calculated the country had an output gap of about 3.0 percent.

The Bank of Canada responded by cautiously lowering Canadian short-term rates by a total of 125 basis points in a series of moves independent of any action by the Fed. The cuts brought the country's key Bank Rate down to 4.25 percent.
As the Bank eased, the Canadian dollar remained steady and money market rates followed -- confirmation of the Bank's independence from Fed policy.

"I think that is clear evidence we have room to set our own monetary policy," said Mark Chandler, senior economist with Goldman Sachs Canada. "This idea that Canada can't have an independent monetary policy, I don't think it holds water."
Now that the Bank of Canada has room to maneuver on domestic monetary policy, investors are questioning what the next move by the Bank will be.
For the most part, analysts agreed the Bank would remain focused on its stated policy goal of keeping the inflation rate, now about 1.4 percent, in a 1.0-3.0 percent range.

Market watchers reckoned the Bank of Canada was at or near the bottom of its interest rate easing cycle. The Bank has reduced rates by 400 basis points since May 1995 and there are indications, such as increases in employment, that the cuts are beginning to take effect.
The Bank is now awaiting further data on the economy rather than risk losing its hard-won credibility with further cuts.
"I think if they wanted to (ease) they could, but I don't think the conditions justify it and I don't think they think conditions justify it," said Goldman's Chandler.

Looking ahead six months, Chandler said it was possible the Bank of Canada could begin raising short-term interest rates, partly in response to a growing Canadian economy and partly in reaction to expected U.S. rate hikes.
"I think it's quite clear we're setting our own monetary policy," said Chandler. "That doesn't mean that Canadian rates won't go up."
-- Reuters Toronto Bureau 416-941-8100
